title: Amazing Grace
composer: Traditional hymn tune “New Britain” (words by John Newton)
about: Count three beats in each bar. The tune starts with one pickup note on beat 3, before the first full bar. In bar 7 the melody climbs to the D above the staff: move your right hand up for it, and back down in bar 10.
source: Melody checked note by note against the Mutopia Project’s “New Britain” hymn setting (SATB, from cyberhymnal.org, public domain). The left hand is our own, simplified from that setting’s bass line. History from Wikipedia.

title: Canon in D
about: The left hand plays the same eight bass notes over and over, two bars at a time, just as the cello does in Pachelbel’s piece. Learn that pattern first: it never changes. Then add the right hand, which plays the first violin part: slow notes at first, then flowing eighth notes.
source: Notes checked note by note against the score of the opening on Wikipedia’s “Pachelbel’s Canon” page (violin I and cello). We keep those two lines for bars 1 to 10 and add a final D chord.

title: Für Elise (first section)
about: This is the famous opening section, with both of its repeats. The whole piece is a rondo that keeps coming back to this music, and our version ends the way the piece ends. The hands take turns: the left hand plays a quick rising chord, then the right hand answers. Keep the E and D-sharp light, like
source: Mutopia Project edition (Stelios Samelis, from Breitkopf & Härtel, 1888; public domain), compared with this file note by note by our checking script. We stop after the second time through bars 10 to 22 and finish with the piece’s last bar. Dates and form from Wikipedia.

title: Greensleeves
about: Count six eighth notes in each bar, in two groups of three. The tune is in E minor. Listen to the refrain: the first time it uses C-sharp (bar 9), and the second time C natural (bar 13), which gives it an old, gentle sound.
source: Melody and bass checked note by note against the Mutopia Project’s “Greensleeves” hymn setting (SATB, from cyberhymnal.org; public domain). We use its top and bottom voices.

title: Gymnopédie No. 1
about: Satie marked it “Lent et douloureux”: slow and sorrowful. In every bar the left hand plays a low bass note and then a soft chord in the middle of the keyboard. The melody floats above with long held notes. The opening chords rock gently between G major 7 and D major 7.
source: Mutopia Project edition (Evin Robertson, from the Dover edition; public domain), compared with this file note by note by our checking script. That edition prints some of the accompaniment chords on the upper staff; here they are on the lower staff, because the left hand plays them. The repeat with first and second endings is as in that edition. Harmony and date from Wikipedia.

title: Hot Cross Buns
about: Three notes and three fingers. Put your right thumb on middle C, finger 2 on D and finger 3 on E, and leave them there the whole time. In bar 3 the notes go twice as fast: these are eighth notes, two to each beat.
source: Traditional tune, played in the three-note form that is usually taught first. Wikipedia notes that the rhyme is sung to more than one tune; no printed score was checked note by note for this one. Date of the words from Wikipedia.

title: Invention No. 1 in C major
about: Bach wrote the Inventions to teach playing two independent lines. The whole piece grows from the short idea in bar 1 (C D E F D E C), which passes back and forth between the hands and is sometimes turned upside down. Practice each hand alone, then put them together slowly.
source: Mutopia Project edition (Jeff Covey, from the Bach-Gesellschaft edition; the typesetting is CC BY-SA 3.0, the music public domain), compared with this file note by note by our checking script. The trills and mordents in that edition are left out.

title: Jingle Bells
about: Pierpont published this song in 1857 as “The One Horse Open Sleigh.” The chorus everyone sings today is a later, simpler tune, and nobody knows who changed it. Keep your right hand still in C position and let the repeated E’s bounce lightly.
source: Chorus checked note by note against an ABC tune file from a University of Calgary computer science course (pages.cpsc.ucalgary.ca), moved down an octave. History from Wikipedia: the original 1857 chorus was different, and today’s chorus was recorded by 1898. The left hand is our own.
license: Public-domain score; app content CC BY-NC 4.0 — Teddy Rook

title: Lightly Row
about: This tune lives in G position: right thumb on the G above middle C, left little finger on the low G. The right hand uses only the five notes under its fingers. The first and last lines skip around the G chord (G, B, D); the middle lines move by step.
source: Melody checked note by note against the “Hänschen klein” page of the German Wikibooks songbook (LilyPond, in D major), moved up to G. English Wikipedia’s article on “Hänschen klein” says its melody is the tune of “Lightly Row”. The left hand is our own and follows that page’s chord symbols.

title: Mary Had a Little Lamb
about: Your right hand stays in C position: thumb on middle C and one finger on each white key up to G. Listen for the notes that repeat. The last bar is a whole note, so hold it for all four beats.
source: Words: Sarah Josepha Hale, Poems for Our Children (1830). Tune: the one it is usually sung to today, also used for “Merrily We Roll Along” (both from Wikipedia). Melody checked against a note-name sheet from the University of California, Riverside (gluckprogram.ucr.edu): four of its five lines match; for bar 4 that sheet uses E E E, a simpler version, and we use the usual E G G.
license: Public-domain score; app content CC BY-NC 4.0 — Teddy Rook

title: Melody
about: The first piece in the album Schumann wrote in 1848 for his three daughters. The right hand sings a slow tune while the left hand flows in eighth notes. Both hands read the treble clef here. Play softly, and let each phrase rise and fall like a sung line.
source: Mutopia Project edition (Philippe Hézaine, from the Peters edition; the music is public domain, the typesetting is CC BY-SA 2.5), compared with this file note by note by our checking script. Fingering and dynamics from that edition. Date from Wikipedia.
license: Public-domain score; app content CC BY-NC 4.0 — Teddy Rook

title: Minuet in G major
composer: Christian Petzold (long credited to J. S. Bach)
about: One of the best-known first pieces. It comes from Anna Magdalena Bach’s music notebook of 1725, and today it is credited to Christian Petzold. Each half is played twice. Keep the quarter notes even and the eighth notes smooth, and let the left hand move calmly underneath.
source: Mutopia Project edition of BWV Anh. 114 (entered by Allen Garvin from the Bach-Gesellschaft edition; public domain), compared with this file note by note by our checking script. The ornaments in that edition (mordents, a trill and a grace note) are left out. Attribution from Wikipedia.

title: Moonlight Sonata, first movement
about: Beethoven asked for the whole movement to be played very delicately and without dampers, which on a modern piano means keeping the pedal down and changing it with the harmony. The right hand does two jobs at once: steady triplets underneath and a slow melody on top, played by the little finger. The
source: Mutopia Project edition (Stewart Holmes, from the 1908 Berners edition edited by A. Winterberger; the typesetting is CC BY-SA 2.5, the music public domain), compared with this file note by note by our checking script. We read the source twice, from its A4 and letter files, and the notes agree. That edition writes some triplets on the lower staff; here every triplet is on the upper staff, played by the right hand. Fingering from that edition. Dates and the meaning of “senza sordino” from Wikipedia.

title: Musette in D major
composer: Anonymous (long credited to J. S. Bach)
about: A musette is a dance named after a small bagpipe, and the left hand imitates its drone by jumping between low and high D. In bars 3 and 4 both hands play the same notes, two octaves apart. Bars 5 to 8 repeat the opening, and each half of the piece is played twice.
source: Mutopia Project edition of BWV Anh. 126 (Allen Garvin, from the Bach-Gesellschaft edition; public domain), compared with this file note by note by our checking script. IMSLP notes that Bach’s authorship is uncertain.
license: Public-domain score; app content CC BY-NC 4.0 — Teddy Rook

title: Ode to Joy
about: Beethoven wrote this tune for the last movement of his Ninth Symphony. It mostly moves by step and stays in C position. In bars 4, 8 and 16, hold the dotted quarter note a little longer and play the short note right after it. In bar 12 your thumb drops down to the G below middle C, then comes back.
source: Melody checked note by note against the Mutopia Project’s “Ode to Joy” hymn setting (SATB, public domain), moved from G down to C. The left hand is our own and follows that setting’s chords.

title: Prelude in C major
about: Every bar is one chord, broken into the same pattern and played twice. The left hand holds its two notes while the right hand plays the rest of the chord. Find each chord shape with your hands first, then play the pattern slowly and evenly. Near the end the bass stays on a low G for eight bars befor
source: Mutopia Project edition (Tobias Erbsland; public domain), compared with this file note by note by our checking script.

title: Prelude in E minor
about: Chopin marked this prelude Largo: very slow. The right hand sings just a few notes, often only B and C, while the left-hand chords sink one half step at a time. Listen to how each new chord changes only one note. The music swells in the middle, then fades into silence before the last chords.
source: Mutopia Project edition (Magnus Lewis-Smith, from the Peters edition, 1879; public domain), compared with this file note by note by our checking script. A turn and two grace notes in that edition are left out. The half-step motion is described in Wikipedia’s article on the prelude.

title: Sonatina in C major, first movement
about: A sonatina is a short sonata, and this is one of the first that piano students learn. Listen for the opening tune: it comes back near the end, an octave lower. Count two half-note beats in each bar (cut time) and keep the scales even.
source: Mutopia Project edition (Brian D. Rude, from the G. Schirmer Sonatina Album, 1893; public domain), compared with this file note by note by our checking script. That edition prints no dynamics in this movement, only the word Spiritoso. Date from Wikipedia.
license: Public-domain score; app content CC BY-NC 4.0 — Teddy Rook

title: The Entertainer (opening)
about: Ragtime sets a steady, march-like left hand against a right hand that lands just off the beat. The left hand jumps: a low bass note on the beat, then a chord in the middle of the keyboard. Practice the left hand alone until the jumps feel easy. Joplin wrote “Not fast” at the top.
source: Mutopia Project edition (Chris Sawer, from a reproduction of the original 1902 edition; public domain), compared with this file note by note by our checking script, except the last bar, where we leave out the three notes that lead into the next strain.
license: Public-domain score; app content CC BY-NC 4.0 — Teddy Rook

title: Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star
composer: Traditional (French tune, 1761; words by Jane Taylor, 1806)
about: The first piece for both hands. The left hand plays one slow note while the right hand sings the tune. Play each hand alone first, then put them together slowly. In the first line your right hand sits a little higher: thumb on C, finger 4 on G and finger 5 on A.
source: Melody checked against the theme of Mozart’s Variations on “Ah vous dirai-je, maman”, K. 265 (Mutopia Project edition for two guitars, from the Porro print; public domain). The notes match. Mozart repeats the note on the long words (“star”, “are”) and adds two small decorations (bars 7 and 15); the song as sung holds a half note there instead. Dates from Wikipedia.
